Boksburg Tigers

By: Busisiwe Gumede | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
White tigers in a Boksburg backyard and neighbours fear that the animals will attack - we investigate why authorities have done nothing about this wildlife hazard.

Unique Selling Point:
In what sounds like something straight out of popular docuseries Tiger King, a couple in Boksburg is keeping two white tigers in their backyard. We use footage shared by the tiger owners, concerned neighbours and animal groups to paint this bizarre picture for the viewer.



Summary:
At the end of September, online news sources began reporting on a Boksburg couple keeping a tiger in their backyard, right next to a daycare centre and not far from an old age home in the area.

After doing research and visiting social media pages of Matthew and Anneline Kruger, we found that it was not one but actually, two white tigers roaming the grounds of the couple's home.

Photos captured by neighbours and animal welfare groups show the tigers loafing dangerously close to the boundary fence and looking over into neighbouring properties.

Neighbours are justifiably concerned for their safety while animal welfare groups say their hands are tied – there is currently no law forbiding the ownership of exotic animals in the City of Ekurhuleni, the municipality under which Boksburg falls.



Further information:
Though there are certain conditions that are put in place for the ownership of such animals, there is no law against the actual ownership. These conditions are detailed under Part 9: Keeping of wild animals in the Ekurhuleni Public Health Bylaws.

But animal welfare groups say the couple is violating at least one of those conditions:

> The enclosure of the animals must not be kept within 50 meters of the boundary fence or any dwelling or building used for human habitation.

It is not clear if the couple has been given notice by the municipality or nature conservation authority to be exempted from the condition above.

We confront the City of Ekurhuleni about what appears to be an oversight in the bylaws and interrogate why nothing has been done to remove the animals despite the obvious safety risk.

Press Release:


Spotted - White Tigers Next Door
In the wild, White Tigers are the ultimate predators, fearlessly stalking their prey for hours before ambushing them and going in for the kill. With their unusual white fur coats these ferocious hunters are in high demand from people wanting exotic pets, but they remain dangerous, wild animals. So, when a pre-school teacher in Boksburg, Gauteng noticed in horror a white tiger peeking through the fence into her creche, she raised the alarm. But, when certain conditions are met, there are no public health bylaws in the City of Ekurhuleni preventing anyone from keeping a wild animal in their own backyard. That’s no comfort to the fearful people who now count two tigers as next-door neighbours.
Producer: Busisiwe Gumede-Chizhanje | Presenter: Macfarlane Moleli

Script:


SCRIPT - Boksburg White Tigers
VO – Nadia Randall is a proud, attentive grandmother of two who is so involved in the lives of her grandchildren - that she had a hand - in choosing the perfect daycare centre for them.
NADIA (SURNAME) – BOKSBURG RESIDENT
00:28 - ... the one is 19 months and the other is 13 months old. 00:46 - We actually looked at a couple of schools before we decided on this one and this school won hands down, absolutely hands down. It’s a good school, a home environment.
VO – But the homely environment at the creche was bizarrely disrupted in September.
NADIA (SURNAME) – BOKSBURG RESIDENT
02:07 - … I actually went to a friend on the 28th and she asked me “do you know about the tigers in Boksburg?” … it’s right behind a nursery school. 02:26 - … she sent the photos and the videos and I was like that’s the school my grandchildren are in!
VO – It turns out, the family next door to the crèche keeps a pair of white tigers in the backyard of their suburban home.
NADIA (SURNAME) – BOKSBURG RESIDENT
05:49 - I’m concerned that they gonna come over the wall or through the wall, not only for my grandchildren, for the other children.
LINK - clip 00:45 - Though found across the globe, white tigers are common in India, Russia and China where they thrive in habitats with low temperatures, swamps and dense jungles. So when residents spotted not one but two of them in Boksburg in Gauteng's East Rand, they were flabbergasted and justifiably horrified.



VO – Crèche owner Tanya Weideman recalls the day staff first saw one of the tigers seated on a high platform, overlooking the school.
UPSOUND - TANYA (SURNAME) – CRÈCHE OWNER
MAC – 02:45 – So it was looking over...
TANYA – At the kids, yes.
MAC - 01:18 - And how many kids come to the daycare center on a daily basis? TANYA - 01:19 - We were, before the tigers, at 62 kids and we are standing now at 52.
VO – To Weideman’s surprise, there wasn't much the authorities could do to intervene.
TANYA (SURNAME) – CRÈCHE OWNER
11:15 - ... from the SPCA to the counsellor, we phoned the municipality, the empd, we phoned ekurhuleni - 11:44 everybody is like, but if they have a permit it’s fine.
VO – That’s because owning a wild animal that is not endemic to South Africa is surprisingly easy in Gauteng, North West, Mpumalanga and Limpopo as no permit is required.
Currently, the Ekurhuleni Municipality’s Public Health Bylaws do not prohibit keeping a tiger as a pet. But, oddly, it’s illegal to house animals that are found in South Africa. Community Activist Audrey Steyn says this makes no sense.
AUDREY STEYN – COMMUNITY ACTIVIST
05:29 - ... in the bylaws tigers have been excluded, so you can’t keep a lion but you can keep a tiger.



VO – The bylaws further state that the enclosure of the animals must not be kept within 50 meters of the boundary fence used for human habitation – a condition that the tiger owners are seemingly violating here. They also aren't considering that their two meter wall isn’t high enough for animals that can jump up to four meters.
AUDREY STEYN – COMMUNITY ACTIVIST
06:30 - ... The enclosure is actually part of the boundary line. 07:05 - So we are really hoping under that law we would be able to get these tigers removed and put them into a sanctuary.
VO – Steyn says the lax bylaws in the East Rand are proving to be quite problematic.
UPSOUND – AUDREY STEYN – COMMUNITY ACTIVIST
MAC - 07:14 - It’s not the first time that you discovered tigers in recent times in this area…
AUDREY - 07:25 - There is tigers in Benoni, Boksburg, Springs and Brakpan. These are in residential areas where people walk their tigers as if they’re walking their dogs.
VO - Since spotting the tigers, some residents were completely shocked and scared that they set up an online petition demanding a review of the by-laws.
LINK - 00:47 - Big cat conservationists say the idea of having cute cubs in the home is so attractive for some people that they discount the fact that white tigers can grow into an impressive weight of 250kg and an intimidating length of 3 meters.
ANDY RIVE – LOVE LIONS SANCTUARY – CLIP 0041
02:36 - They are the largest of the big cats and there is no way that you can domesticate them. … and even when you look on the internet and any of these people interacting with these cats, that animal is climbing on top of those guys. ... That cat is practicing hunting. There is no way that you could ever tame or domesticate or expect them not to at some point show their real behaviour and their instinctual behaviour .
VO – In 2015 Andy Rive and Line Risa established the Love Lions Alive Sanctuary in Swinburne, in Freestate - a 3-hour drive from Johannesburg. Andy says keeping tigers in a suburban backyard is never a good idea.



ANDY RIVE – LOVE LIONS SANCTUARY – CLIP 0041
02:29 - To have constant sound and even traffic and the smoke and smell of everything that comes along with being in a city in the Joburg area, to hear those children all the time... 02:22 - They are being tempted all the time by what’s going on around them, it’s not safe.
MAC - 06:50 - Who is letting us down here? Is it the government, is it legislation, how are people getting away with this?
ANDY - 07:42 ... I think that it’s government. 07:52 - Even though government knows about tigers being in the suburbs and has known for many years, nothing is being done yet. ...They are not stopping it because there is no legislation.
VO – For the wellbeing of the tigers and safety of the caregivers, a lot of effort goes into the construction of wild cat enclosures.
ANDY RIVE – LOVE LIONS SANCTUARY – CLIP 0041
02:01 - ... we use the diamond fence three meters tall, one meter overhang and we have 19 to 23 electric strands on it. 02:13 - The electricity is very important. That’s what stops them from wanting to even come out and it’s pegged into the ground , the electrics stop them from wanting to dig.
VO – The sanctuary tries to create an environment as similar as possible to the natural habitat of its wild cats.
ANDY RIVE – LOVE LIONS SANCTUARY – CLIP 0041
00:18 - Tigers want forest it’s part of their natural environment. We’ve built his enclosure where there is natural rock and mountainous area.
LINK – clip 0032.MXF – 00:23 - So this is what a proper enclosure should look like if you want to keep a tiger in some sort of enclosure, this is about three meters high and another meter above of electric fencing, giving it about four meters but even if you speak to the people in this sanctuary they will tell you that all a tiger wants to do is come out because
